name: SeamlessM4T
description: SeamlessM4T (Massively Multilingual & Multimodal Machine Translation) is a unified model that supports speech-to-speech translation, speech-to-text translation, text-to-speech translation, text-to-text translation, and automatic speech recognition for up to 100 languages. The model uses 1 million hours of open speech audio data to learn self-supervised speech representations with w2v-BERT 2.0 and creates a multimodal corpus of automatically aligned speech translations dubbed SeamlessAlign.
creator: Meta AI Research
inLanguage: 100 languages for speech source, 95 languages for text source and target
citeAs: Seamless Communication et al., SeamlessM4T: Massively Multilingual & Multimodal Machine Translation, arXiv:2308.11596v3, 2023
rai:dataCollection: The data collection process involved gathering 4 million hours of raw audio from a publicly available repository of crawled web data, followed by deduplication, downloading, resampling at 16KHz, and filtering non-speech data with an audio event detection model. Audio segmentation was performed using Voice Activity Detection (VAD) to split files into shorter segments. Speech mining was conducted using SONAR embeddings to create aligned speech translations. Text data was drawn from NLLB datasets with the same data sources, cleaning, and filtering steps.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw audio data originated from a publicly available repository of crawled web data totaling 4 million hours. Text data was sourced from NLLB datasets. Human-labeled S2TT data came from open-source datasets including CoVoST 2, MuST-C, EuroParl-ST, and VoxPopuli. ASR data was collected from various open-source and licensed datasets with at least 100 hours of ASR transcriptions for most languages.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio files were deduplicated by URL, downloaded, and resampled at 16KHz. Non-speech data was filtered using an audio event detection (AED) model. Audio segmentation was performed using Voice Activity Detection (VAD) followed by over-segmentation to create multiple overlapping splits. Speech language identification (LID) was applied to each segment. For text, special tokens were removed from verbatim transcriptions, and length filtering was applied to remove examples exceeding 100 sub-word tokens and pairs with skewed text-to-audio length ratios exceeding 5 sub-words per second.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing steps included: (1) Audio resampling to 16KHz, (2) Voice Activity Detection for segmentation, (3) Speech language identification using a custom LID model, (4) Over-segmentation creating overlapping splits, (5) Text tokenization using SentencePiece with BPE algorithm on a 256K-sized vocabulary, (6) Length filtering removing utterances shorter than 0.1 seconds or longer than 50 seconds and text longer than 250 sub-words, (7) Toxicity filtering removing pairs with toxicity imbalance above threshold of 1, (8) Filtering pairs with more than 20% emojis, 50% punctuation, or 50% spaces. For S2ST data, filtering based on seconds of audio per text token length ratio was applied, discarding pairs with ratio exceeding 0.5.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human annotations were collected for ASR transcriptions with at least 100 hours per language for most languages. For S2TT evaluation, human annotations were collected using the XSTS protocol where 3 annotators examined each source-target pair and evaluated semantic similarity on a 1-5 scale. In cases of disagreement of 2 or more score values, 2 additional annotators evaluated the same item. For S2ST evaluation, MOS protocol was used with annotators providing Likert scores (1-5) for clarity of speech, sound quality, and naturalness. Pseudo-labeling was performed by using NLLB-200-3.3B to generate translations of ASR data.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For XSTS annotations, the median score over annotators was taken for each evaluation sentence pair for robustness. Calibration was performed using a monolingual cross-lingual calibration set with moderated calibration methodology to reduce language-level annotator biases. Annotator crews sufficiently out of calibration were identified for exclusion or additional training. For disagreements in XSTS scores of 2 or more points, additional annotators were consulted bringing the total to 5 evaluator scores.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The models (SeamlessM4T-Large with 2.3B parameters and SeamlessM4T-Medium with 1.2B parameters) are released as open-source with model weights, inference code, and fine-tuning recipes. Metadata to recreate the unfiltered 470,000 hours of SeamlessAlign is provided. The release includes Stopes-based pipelines for creating alignments and SONAR for speech encoders in 37 languages and text encoders in 200 languages. The automatic evaluation model Blaser 2.0 is also released with model weights and inference scripts.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The HolisticBias dataset used for evaluation covers demographic axes including ability, age, body type, characteristics, cultural, gender and sex, nationality, political ideologies, race/ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, and socioeconomic class. Gender representation analysis was conducted using gendered nouns and pronouns from HolisticBias. The Fleurs dataset contains speech recordings from multiple speakers with varying gender distributions across languages (53% gender-matched pairings, 47% mixed-gender matches).
rai:dataSocialImpact: The work aims to augment world-readiness by enabling multilingual communication across various contexts. It can support individuals with accessibility needs including those who lack reading/writing skills or are blind/visually impaired. The system addresses script variance issues for languages with multiple writing systems. However, the distribution of benefits may vary based on user demographics and social situation. ASR performance may vary based on gender, race, accent, or language. The system's performance on slang or proper nouns may be inconsistent across high and low-resource languages.
rai:dataBiases: Gender bias evaluation revealed that SeamlessM4T exhibits an average preference of approximately 10% towards translating to masculine forms when no gender information is available in the source sentence. When translating from gendered sentences, the model shows a lack of robustness with approximately 3% variation when gender is altered. Masculine representation is predominant in most training datasets. The model shows overgeneralization towards masculine forms and reduced translation quality when using feminine references. Different demographic axes show varying levels of added toxicity, with cultural, body type, socioeconomic class, and religion being most sensitive categories.
rai:dataLimitations: Known limitations include: (1) The model is trained on general domain data and not intended for domain-specific inputs like medical or legal domains, (2) Not intended for long-form translation as it was trained on short text and speech inputs, (3) Translations cannot be used as certified translations, (4) Performance may vary based on speaker demographics including gender, race, and accent, (5) Inconsistent performance on slang and proper nouns across high and low-resource languages, (6) Speech-to-speech translation carries higher interactional risks due to limited ability for users to ascertain output quality or make edits in live conversations, (7) Truncations and omissions observed in S2ST outputs particularly for longer audio durations, (8) Word list-based toxicity detection has limitations including over-detection in specific contexts and reliance on precise tokenization, (9) ASR adds additional errors when used for evaluation metrics like ASR-BLEU, (10) Zero-shot evaluation for 34 out of 101 language directions in some tasks.
rai:dataUseCases: Primary intended uses include research in speech and text translation supporting: (1) ASR for 96 languages, (2) S2ST from 100 source speech languages into 35 target speech languages, (3) S2TT from 100 source speech languages into 95 target text languages, (4) T2ST from 95 source text languages into 35 target speech languages, (5) T2TT from 95 source text languages into 95 target text languages, (6) TTS for 36 languages. The model is intended for research purposes and not for production deployment. Usage guidelines specify it should be viewed as an augmentation device assisting translation rather than replacing language learning or human interpreters, especially in high-stakes situations involving legal or medical decision-making.
rai:annotationsPerItem: For XSTS evaluation, 3 annotators examined each source-target pair initially, with up to 5 total annotators for items with disagreement of 2 or more score values. For MOS evaluation, 3 annotators scored each generation for most languages, with some languages receiving scores from only a single annotator per item.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotators went through monolingual English practice evaluations with score justifications prior to annotation. More than 3 (up to 30) annotators were used per language pair for XSTS evaluation. For MOS evaluation in the X-eng direction, 31 annotators evaluated items from each input language. Specific demographic information about annotators is not provided.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Pseudo-labeling was performed using NLLB-200-3.3B for generating translations of ASR data. Whisper-Large-v2 and Whisper-Medium were used for ASR transcription in evaluation metrics (ASR-BLEU). YourTTS was used for text-to-speech synthesis in baseline cascaded systems. MMS-TTS was used to extend text-based datasets to speech modality. ETOX with Toxicity-200 word lists was used for toxicity detection. XLS-R-1B was used to extract discrete acoustic units from speech. HiFi-GAN vocoders were used for speech synthesis from units.
